22862.e: “Velox” means swift and “raptor” means robber. It was a quick hunter.

22863.q: On how many legs did Velociraptor run?
22863.e: Velociraptor ran on its two back legs. It did not need its arms for running.

22864.q: With which dinosaur was a Velociraptor found fossilised in the middle of a fight?
22864.e: A famous fossil shows a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops fighting each other. Both were buried together.
22864.m: A Velociraptor was fossilised fighting a Protoceratops.

22865.q: What was especially long on Diplodocus?
22865.e: Diplodocus had a long neck and an even longer tail.
22865.m: Diplodocus had a long neck and tail.

22866.q: Roughly how long was a Diplodocus?
22866.e: A Diplodocus grew to about 25 metres long. That is longer than two buses.
22866.m: A Diplodocus was about 25 metres long.

22867.q: What did the teeth of Diplodocus look like?
22867.e: Its teeth were as thin as pegs and sat at the front of its mouth. It used them to strip off leaves.

22868.q: How might Diplodocus have used its tail?
22868.e: Scientists think it could swing the thin tip of its tail like a whip.
22868.m: Diplodocus could probably swing its tail like a whip.

22869.q: What is the famous Diplodocus cast from the Natural History Museum in London called?
22869.e: The cast is called “Dippy”. It stood in the museum's entrance hall for many years.
22869.m: The Diplodocus cast from London is called Dippy.

22870.e: People used to think such big animals lived in water. Today we know that Diplodocus lived on land.

22871.q: What does the name Diplodocus mean?
22871.e: The name means “double beam”. It refers to special bones under its tail.

22872.q: How did Diplodocus carry its long tail when walking?
a: In the air above the ground
22872.e: Fossil footprints show no marks of a tail dragging. So Diplodocus held its tail in the air.
22872.m: Diplodocus carried its tail in the air.

22873.e: With its heavy body and short legs it was probably rather slow. Because of its protection, it did not need to run away.

22874.q: What was the back of Ankylosaurus covered with?
22874.e: Many hard bony plates and knobs covered its back. They protected it from bites.
22874.m: The back of Ankylosaurus was covered with bony plates.

22875.e: Ankylosaurus was a plant eater. Because it was built so low, it ate plants close to the ground.

22876.q: How was the body of Ankylosaurus built?
22876.e: Its body was wide and low to the ground. That made it hard to knock over.

a: At the end of the Cretaceous
At the time of the lake dwellers
22877.e: Ankylosaurus lived about 68 to 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous.
22877.m: Ankylosaurus lived at the end of the Cretaceous.

22878.q: On which continent did Ankylosaurus live?
22878.e: Ankylosaurus fossils have been found in western North America.

22879.q: Roughly how long was an Ankylosaurus?
22879.e: Depending on the estimate, an Ankylosaurus was about 6 to 9 metres long.
22879.m: An Ankylosaurus was about 8 metres long.

22880.q: What does the name Ankylosaurus mean?
22880.e: The name means “fused lizard”. Many of its bones were firmly joined together.

22881.q: What did Spinosaurus have on its back?
22881.e: It had a tall sail on its back. It was held up by long bony spines.
22881.m: Spinosaurus had a sail on its back.

22882.e: Spinosaurus mainly ate fish. But it probably also caught other animals.

22883.q: What did the snout of Spinosaurus look like?
22883.e: Its snout was long and narrow like a crocodile's. It was good for grabbing fish.
22883.m: Spinosaurus had a snout like a crocodile.

22884.e: Its fossils have been found in Egypt and Morocco. Both countries are in North Africa.

22885.q: According to current knowledge, which of these predatory dinosaurs was the longest?
22885.e: Depending on the estimate, Spinosaurus grew to about 13 to 16 metres long. It is thought to be one of the longest predatory dinosaurs.
22885.m: Spinosaurus was one of the longest predatory dinosaurs.

22886.q: Where did Spinosaurus often spend its time?
22886.e: Spinosaurus lived by large rivers. It could probably swim well too.
22886.m: Spinosaurus spent a lot of time in water.

22887.q: What happened to the first Spinosaurus bones in a museum in Munich?
a: They were destroyed in the war
22887.e: The first bones were destroyed in 1944 during the Second World War in a bombing raid. Luckily, there were drawings of them.
22887.m: The first Spinosaurus bones were destroyed in the war.

22888.q: What does the name Spinosaurus mean?
22888.e: “Spina” means spine or thorn. The name suits the long bones that held up its back sail.

22889.q: What did Parasaurolophus have on its head?
22889.e: On its head it had a long, curved crest made of bone. It was hollow inside.
22889.m: Parasaurolophus had a long crest on its head.

22890.q: What was the head crest of Parasaurolophus probably for?
22890.e: Long tubes ran through the hollow crest. It could probably use them to make loud, deep sounds, like a trombone.
22890.m: Parasaurolophus probably made sounds with its crest.

22891.e: Parasaurolophus was a plant eater. It ground up leaves and twigs with lots of teeth.

22892.q: Which group does Parasaurolophus belong to?
22892.e: It belongs to the hadrosaurs. They are also called duck-billed dinosaurs because the front of their mouth was wide and flat.

22893.q: On which continent did Parasaurolophus live?
22893.e: Parasaurolophus fossils have been found in Canada and the USA.

a: On two or on four legs
22894.e: It could walk on all fours. To run fast, it probably stood up on its back legs.
22894.m: Parasaurolophus walked on two or four legs.

22895.q: Roughly how long was a Parasaurolophus?
22895.e: A fully grown Parasaurolophus was about 9 to 10 metres long.
22895.m: A Parasaurolophus was about 9 metres long.

22896.q: In which period of Earth's history did Parasaurolophus live?
22896.e: Parasaurolophus lived about 76 to 73 million years ago in the Cretaceous.

22897.q: What did Iguanodon have on its thumb?
22897.e: Its thumb was a sharp spike. It may have used it for defence.

22898.q: Where did scientists first think the thumb spike of Iguanodon belonged?
22898.e: At first people thought the spike was a horn on its nose. Only later skeleton finds showed that it belonged to the thumb.
22898.m: Iguanodon's thumb spike was first thought to be a nose horn.

22899.q: What does the name Iguanodon mean?
22899.e: Its teeth look like very large iguana teeth. That is why it got this name.

22900.q: In which country were the first Iguanodon teeth found?
22900.e: The first teeth were found in southern England. The doctor Gideon Mantell named the animal in 1825.
22900.m: The first Iguanodon teeth were found in England.

22901.q: In which country were many Iguanodon skeletons found in a coal mine?
22901.e: In 1878, miners at Bernissart in Belgium found the skeletons of about 30 animals. Many of them are now in a museum in Brussels.
22901.m: Many Iguanodon skeletons were found in Belgium.

22902.e: Iguanodon was a plant eater. It bit off plants with its beak and chewed them.

22903.q: What is Iguanodon famous for in science?
a: It was one of the first dinosaurs to be named
22903.e: Iguanodon was only the second dinosaur ever to be given a scientific name.
22903.m: Iguanodon is one of the first known dinosaurs.

22904.q: Roughly how long was a large Iguanodon?
22904.e: A large Iguanodon was about 8 to 10 metres long and weighed several tonnes.
22904.m: An Iguanodon was about 9 metres long.

22905.q: Were newly hatched dinosaurs as big as their parents?
22905.e: After all, the babies fitted inside an egg. They still had to grow for many years before they were as big as their parents.
22905.m: Baby dinosaurs were much smaller than their parents.

22906.q: Where did many dinosaurs lay their eggs?
22906.e: Many dinosaurs dug nests in the ground and laid their eggs in them.
22906.m: Many dinosaurs laid their eggs in nests on the ground.

22907.q: Which dinosaur is called “good mother lizard” because it looked after its young?
22907.e: Nests with young animals were found for Maiasaura. The parents probably brought them food.

22908.q: The name Oviraptor means “egg thief”. What was it really doing with the eggs?
a: It was brooding its own eggs
It was stealing other animals' eggs
It was burying other animals' eggs
22908.e: An Oviraptor was found sitting on a nest. They were its own eggs, which it was keeping warm and protecting.
22908.m: Oviraptor was not an egg thief; it was brooding.

22909.q: In which desert were famous nests with dinosaur eggs discovered in 1923?
22909.e: In 1923, an expedition from New York found nests with fossilised eggs in the Gobi Desert.
22909.m: Famous dinosaur nests were found in the Gobi Desert.

22910.q: Roughly how big were the eggs of the giant long-necked dinosaurs?
a: About as big as a grapefruit
About as big as a car
About as big as a bathtub
About as big as a fridge
22910.e: Even the biggest dinosaurs laid quite small eggs. Their eggs were about as big as a grapefruit.
22910.m: Giant dinosaurs laid surprisingly small eggs.

22911.q: What has been found inside some fossilised dinosaur eggs?
22911.e: Some eggs contain tiny bones of unhatched babies. This shows which species laid the egg.
22911.m: Some dinosaur eggs contain baby bones.

22912.q: How many eggs did many dinosaurs lay in a nest?
a: Only one egg in their whole life
22912.e: Many nests have several eggs lying next to each other, often arranged in a circle.
22912.m: Dinosaurs often laid lots of eggs in a nest.

22913.q: How did some dinosaurs probably keep their eggs warm?
22913.e: Scientists think some dinosaurs covered their eggs with plants and earth. As the plants rotted, they gave off heat.

22914.q: What kind of teeth did meat-eating dinosaurs have?
22914.e: Meat eaters had pointed, curved teeth with small serrations. They could tear meat with them.

22915.q: Why did many plant-eating dinosaurs have a very big belly?
a: To digest plants for a long time
22915.e: Plants are hard to digest. That is why the plant eaters needed a long gut and a big belly.
22915.m: Plant eaters needed a big belly for digestion.

22916.q: Which plants did many plant-eating dinosaurs eat?
22916.e: At that time, mainly ferns, horsetails and conifers grew. Many plant eaters fed on them.
22916.m: Many dinosaurs ate ferns and conifers.

22917.q: Why did some plant-eating dinosaurs swallow stones?
22917.e: The stones in the stomach probably helped to grind up tough plants. Chickens do something similar today.
22917.m: Some dinosaurs swallowed stones to help digestion.

22918.q: What did most species of dinosaur eat?
22918.e: There were many more species of plant eaters than of meat eaters.

22919.q: What does fossilised dinosaur poo tell scientists?
22919.e: Fossilised poo contains remains of bones or plants. This shows what the animal ate.
22919.m: Fossilised poo shows what a dinosaur ate.

22920.q: How did many plant eaters protect themselves from meat eaters?
a: With horns, armour or by living in herds
22920.e: Some plant eaters had horns or armour. Others lived in large groups, where they were safer.
22920.m: Plant eaters protected themselves with horns, armour or herds.

22921.q: What do we call animals that eat plants and meat?
22921.e: Omnivores eat both plants and meat. There were probably omnivores among the dinosaurs too.

22922.q: Which of these dinosaurs was one of the biggest of all?
22922.e: Argentinosaurus from South America was a giant long-necked dinosaur. It is one of the biggest land animals of all time.
22922.m: Argentinosaurus was one of the biggest dinosaurs.

22923.e: Scientists estimate its length at about 30 to 35 metres. That is as long as three buses one behind the other.
22923.m: Argentinosaurus was more than 30 metres long.

22924.q: Roughly how heavy were the biggest long-necked dinosaurs?
22924.e: The biggest long-necked dinosaurs probably weighed 50 to 70 tonnes. An African elephant weighs about 6 tonnes.
22924.m: The biggest dinosaurs weighed as much as many elephants.

22925.q: Which dinosaur was only about as big as a chicken?
22925.e: Compsognathus was about 1 metre long, much of it tail. It weighed only a few kilograms.
22925.m: Compsognathus was a very small dinosaur.

22926.q: Roughly how long was a Tyrannosaurus rex?
22926.e: The biggest T. rex found were about 12 metres long, as long as a bus.
22926.m: A T. rex was about 12 metres long.

22927.q: How do scientists find out how big a dinosaur was?
a: They measure the height of caves
22927.e: From the length of the bones, scientists can estimate size and weight.
22927.m: Scientists measure bones to estimate size.

22928.q: Which group of dinosaurs did the very biggest animals belong to?
22928.e: The biggest dinosaurs were sauropods with long necks and tails. No other land animal ever grew so big.
22928.m: The biggest dinosaurs were long-necked dinosaurs.

22929.q: Which animal living today is heavier than almost all dinosaurs?
22929.e: A blue whale can weigh well over 100 tonnes. It is one of the heaviest animals that has ever lived.
22929.m: The blue whale is heavier than almost all dinosaurs.

22930.q: Roughly how heavy was a Tyrannosaurus rex?
a: As heavy as a large elephant
22930.e: A fully grown T. rex weighed about 8 to 9 tonnes. That is roughly as much as a large elephant.
22930.m: A T. rex was about as heavy as a large elephant.

22931.e: Pteranodon was a pterosaur. It soared through the air on large wings.

22932.q: How did Pteranodon move on the ground?
22932.e: Fossil footprints show that pterosaurs walked on all fours on the ground. They leaned on their folded wings.
22932.m: On the ground, Pteranodon walked on all fours.

22933.q: Did Pteranodon have teeth in its beak?
22933.e: The name Pteranodon means “wing without tooth”. Its long beak had no teeth.
22933.m: Pteranodon had a beak without teeth.

22934.q: What did Pteranodon have on the back of its head?
22934.e: A long crest of bone stuck out backwards from the back of its head. In some animals, probably the males, it was especially large.
22934.m: Pteranodon had a bony crest on its head.

22935.e: Pteranodon flew over the sea and caught fish. Fish remains have even been found with its fossils.

22936.q: What were the wings of Pteranodon made of?
22936.e: The wings were a thin membrane of skin. It was stretched out on a very long finger.
22936.m: Pterosaurs flew with wings made of skin.

22937.q: How big was the wingspan of a large Pteranodon?
22937.e: Large animals had a wingspan of about 6 to 7 metres. That is wider than a car is long.

22938.q: On which continent have most Pteranodon fossils been found?
22938.e: Most finds come from the US state of Kansas. There was a sea there a long time ago.
22938.m: Pteranodon has mainly been found in North America.

22939.e: Ichthyosaurs were reptiles that lived entirely in water. They never came onto land.

22940.q: Which animal living today did ichthyosaurs look like?
22940.e: Ichthyosaurs had a long snout, a streamlined body and a back fin. Dolphins look like that too.

22941.e: Fossils of mothers with young inside their bodies have been found. The young were born directly in the water.
22941.m: Ichthyosaurs gave birth to live young.

22942.q: What did ichthyosaurs have to do at the surface of the water?
22942.e: Ichthyosaurs had lungs and no gills. That is why they had to come up to breathe.

22943.q: What was especially big on ichthyosaurs?
22943.e: Ichthyosaurs had huge eyes. With them they could see well even in dark, deep water.

22944.q: What did ichthyosaurs have instead of legs?
22944.e: Their legs had changed into flippers. They used them to steer in the water.
22944.m: Ichthyosaurs had flippers instead of legs.

22945.q: What did ichthyosaurs mainly use to push themselves along when swimming?
22945.e: Ichthyosaurs had a strong tail fin like a fish. With it they swam fast.
22945.m: Ichthyosaurs swam with their tail fin.

22946.q: What does the name ichthyosaur mean?
22946.e: The Greek word “ichthys” means fish and “sauros” means lizard.

22947.q: What was especially long on many plesiosaurs?
22947.e: Many plesiosaurs had a very long neck. They could use it to snap at prey.
22947.m: Many plesiosaurs had a long neck.

22948.q: How many flippers did a plesiosaur have?
22948.e: Plesiosaurs had two flippers at the front and two at the back. They moved them like paddles.

22949.q: How big was the head of a long-necked plesiosaur?
22949.e: A small head sat at the end of the long neck. It was full of sharp teeth.
22949.m: Long-necked plesiosaurs had a small head.

22950.q: Which legendary creature do plesiosaurs remind many people of?
22950.e: Nessie is said to live in a lake in Scotland. Many people imagine her looking like a plesiosaur.
22950.m: Nessie is often drawn like a plesiosaur.

22951.e: Plesiosaurs lived in the sea at the time of the dinosaurs. But they were reptiles of a separate group.
22951.m: Plesiosaurs are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.

22952.e: Plesiosaurs were predators. They held on to slippery prey with their sharp teeth.

22953.q: When did the plesiosaurs die out?
a: At the same time as the dinosaurs
22953.e: The plesiosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous. The large dinosaurs also disappeared then.
22953.m: Plesiosaurs died out with the dinosaurs.

22954.q: Which plesiosaur had an especially long neck?
22954.e: Elasmosaurus had more than 70 neck bones. Its neck was longer than the whole rest of its body.
22954.m: Elasmosaurus had an extremely long neck.

22955.e: Archaeopteryx is one of the oldest known birds. That is why it is called the first bird.
22955.m: Archaeopteryx is the famous first bird.

22956.q: What did Archaeopteryx have on its body?
22956.e: Clear prints of feathers can be seen in the stones. Its wings had feathers too.
22956.m: Archaeopteryx had feathers like a bird.

22957.q: What did Archaeopteryx have in its mouth, unlike birds today?
22957.e: Birds today have no teeth. Archaeopteryx still had small sharp teeth like a reptile.

22958.q: What did Archaeopteryx have on its wings?
22958.e: On each wing it had three fingers with claws. It may have used them to hold on.
22958.m: Archaeopteryx had claws on its wings.

22959.q: What was the tail of Archaeopteryx like?
22959.e: Archaeopteryx had a long tail with many vertebrae. Feathers grew on both sides.
22959.m: Archaeopteryx had a long bony tail.

22960.q: Between which groups of animals is Archaeopteryx seen as a link?
22960.e: Archaeopteryx shows features of both groups. That is why it is so important for science.

22961.e: Archaeopteryx was about as big as a raven. So it was a fairly small animal.
22961.m: Archaeopteryx was about the size of a raven.

22962.q: In which rock are the fossils of Archaeopteryx preserved?
22962.e: The finds are in fine slabs of limestone. Even the feathers can be seen clearly in them.

22963.q: What was special about the sabre-toothed cat?
22963.e: Its upper canine teeth were long and curved like a sabre. That is where its name comes from.
22963.m: Sabre-toothed cats had huge canine teeth.

22964.q: What is the best-known sabre-toothed cat called?
22964.e: Smilodon is the most famous sabre-toothed cat. It was about as big as a lion or bigger.
22964.m: The best-known sabre-toothed cat is called Smilodon.

a: At the time of the trilobites
22965.e: Smilodon lived in the Ice Age. It died out about 10,000 years ago.
22965.m: Smilodon lived in the Ice Age.

22966.q: Where did many sabre-toothed cats get stuck and so become fossils?
22966.e: Thousands of bones were found in the La Brea Tar Pits. The animals got stuck in the sticky tar.
22966.m: Many sabre-toothed cats were found in tar pits.

22967.e: Smilodon was a powerful hunter. It caught large animals such as bison or horses.

22968.q: What was the tail of Smilodon like?
22968.e: Smilodon had a short tail, rather like a lynx. Lions today have a long tail.

22969.q: In which part of the world did Smilodon live?
22969.e: Smilodon lived in North and South America. Its bones have been found there.

22970.q: Does the sabre-toothed cat still exist today?
22970.e: Sabre-toothed cats died out a long time ago. We only know them from bones and skulls.

22971.q: What protected the woolly rhinoceros from the cold?
22971.e: The woolly rhinoceros had long, woolly fur. This helped it survive the icy cold.
22971.m: The woolly rhinoceros had a thick woolly coat.

22972.q: How many horns did the woolly rhinoceros have?
22972.e: There was a long horn at the front of its nose. A smaller second horn grew behind it.
22972.m: The woolly rhinoceros had two horns.

22973.q: What did the woolly rhinoceros eat?
22973.e: The woolly rhinoceros was a plant eater. It grazed on grass on the cold steppe.

22974.q: Where have woolly rhinos been found with their skin and hair?
a: In warm sand by a river
At the bottom of a lake
22974.e: In Siberia the ground is frozen all year round. Some animals there were preserved almost as if in a freezer.
22974.m: Frozen ground can preserve Ice Age animals.

22975.q: Who painted woolly rhinos on cave walls?
22975.e: There are old paintings of woolly rhinos in caves in France. They were made by Stone Age people.
22975.m: Stone Age people painted woolly rhinos.

22976.q: Where did the woolly rhinoceros live?
22976.e: The woolly rhinoceros lived on the cold steppes from Europe to Asia. There were no woolly rhinos in America.
22976.m: The woolly rhinoceros lived in Europe and Asia.

22977.q: How did the woolly rhinoceros usually hold its head?
22977.e: Its head hung low, rather like today's white rhino. That made it easy to eat grass.
22977.m: The woolly rhinoceros held its head low.

22978.q: How big could the giant ground sloth Megatherium get?
22978.e: Megatherium weighed several tonnes. Standing upright, it was much taller than a person.
22978.m: The giant ground sloth was as big as an elephant.

22979.e: Megatherium lived in South America. Many of its bones have been found there.

22980.q: What did the giant ground sloth eat?
22980.e: Giant ground sloths were plant eaters. They pulled off leaves and twigs.
22980.m: The giant ground sloth ate plants.

22981.q: How did the giant ground sloth reach high leaves?
a: It stood up on its back legs
22981.e: The giant ground sloth propped itself up on its back legs and its thick tail. That way it reached high branches.
22981.m: The giant ground sloth could stand upright.

22982.q: What did the giant ground sloth have on its front feet?
22982.e: It used its long claws to pull branches towards it. The claws were very strong.
22982.m: The giant ground sloth had long claws.

22983.q: Where did the giant ground sloth mainly move about?
22983.e: Sloths today hang in trees. The giant ground sloth was far too heavy for that and walked on the ground.
22983.m: The giant ground sloth lived on the ground.

22984.q: Which famous scientist found bones of giant ground sloths?
22984.e: Charles Darwin travelled around the world on the ship Beagle. In Argentina he dug up bones of giant ground sloths.
22984.m: Charles Darwin found giant ground sloth bones.

22985.q: In which cave near Vättis in the canton of St Gallen were cave bear bones found?
22985.e: The Drachenloch lies high above Vättis. Many cave bear bones were found there.
22985.m: Cave bear bones were found in the Drachenloch.

22986.q: What did the cave bear mainly eat?
22986.e: Studies of its teeth and bones show that it fed mainly on plants.
22986.m: The cave bear mainly ate plants.

22987.q: What traces did cave bears leave on cave walls?
22987.e: In many caves you can still see scratch marks from bear claws on the walls today. The bears probably sharpened their claws there.
22987.m: Cave bears left scratch marks in caves.

22988.q: How big was the cave bear compared with today's brown bear?
22988.e: The cave bear was heavier and stronger than most brown bears today.
22988.m: The cave bear was bigger than a brown bear.

22989.q: In which cave in the Alpstein were cave bear bones found?
22989.e: The Wildkirchli is in the Alpstein in Appenzell Innerrhoden. Cave bear bones and tools of Stone Age people were found there. The Kesslerloch is near Thayngen, the Höllgrotten near Baar and the Drachenloch near Vättis.
22989.m: The Wildkirchli is a well-known site in the Alpstein.

22990.q: When did the cave bear die out?
22990.e: The cave bear died out during the last Ice Age, about 25,000 years ago.
22990.m: The cave bear died out in the Ice Age.

22991.q: Did cave bears live at the same time as Stone Age people?
22991.e: Cave bears and Stone Age people lived in Europe at the same time. Sometimes both used the same caves.
22991.m: Cave bears and Stone Age people lived at the same time.

22992.q: What was especially big on the giant deer?
22992.e: The giant deer had the biggest antlers of any known deer.
22992.m: The giant deer had enormous antlers.

22993.q: How wide could the antlers of the giant deer be?
22993.e: From one tip to the other, the antlers could be up to about 3.6 metres wide. That is wider than a car.
22993.m: The antlers of the giant deer were more than 3 metres wide.

22994.e: As with most deer, only the males had antlers.
22994.m: Only male giant deer had antlers.

22995.q: What is the giant deer also called, because it was often found in Ireland?
22995.e: Many well-preserved skeletons were found in Irish bogs. Despite the name, it was not an elk.
22995.m: The giant deer is also called the Irish elk.

22996.q: What did the giant deer do with its antlers every year?
22996.e: Deer shed their antlers every year. Then new ones grow.
22996.m: The giant deer grew new antlers every year.

22997.q: What did the giant deer eat?
22997.e: Like all deer, the giant deer was a plant eater.

22998.q: Which deer living today is closely related to the giant deer?
22998.e: Studies show that the fallow deer is a close relative.
22998.m: The fallow deer is a relative of the giant deer.

22999.q: How big was the dawn horse?
a: About as big as a fox
As big as a horse today
22999.e: The dawn horse was only about as big as a fox. Horses only became big later.
22999.m: The dawn horse was as small as a fox.

23000.q: How many toes did the dawn horse have on its front legs?
23000.e: The dawn horse had four toes at the front and three at the back. It walked on them over soft forest floor.
23000.m: The dawn horse had four toes at the front.

23001.q: How many toes does a horse today have on each leg?
23001.e: Horses today walk on just one single toe. It is inside the hard hoof.
23001.m: A horse walks on one toe with a hoof.

23002.q: Where did the dawn horse live?
23002.e: The dawn horse lived in warm forests. There were hardly any wide grasslands at that time.
23002.m: The dawn horse lived in the forest.

23003.q: What did the dawn horse eat?
23003.e: The dawn horse ate soft leaves and fruit from the forest.
23003.m: The dawn horse ate leaves and fruit.

23004.q: How do we know today what the dawn horse looked like?
a: From dawn horses in the forest
From frozen animals in the ice
23004.e: Bones of the dawn horse were preserved in rock. In the Messel Pit in Germany, whole skeletons have even been found.
23004.m: We know the dawn horse from fossils.

23005.q: How long ago did the dawn horse live?
23005.e: The dawn horse lived about 50 million years ago. That was long before the first humans.
23005.m: The dawn horse lived about 50 million years ago.

23006.q: Did the dawn horse live at the time of the dinosaurs?
a: Yes, at exactly the same time
23006.e: The large dinosaurs had already died out when the dawn horse lived.
23006.m: The dawn horse lived after the dinosaurs.

23007.e: Trilobites crawled and swam on the sea floor. Their fossils are found in old marine rocks.

23008.q: Into how many parts is a trilobite's body divided lengthways?
23008.e: The name trilobite means “three-lobed”. The body has a middle part and two side parts.

23009.q: What protected the body of trilobites?
23009.e: Trilobites had a hard shell on their back. That is why they are so well preserved as fossils.

23010.q: What could many trilobites do when in danger?
23010.e: Many trilobites rolled up into a ball like a woodlouse. This protected their soft underside.

23011.q: What kind of eyes did many trilobites have?
23011.e: Their eyes were made of many small lenses of calcite. Eyes like this are called compound eyes.

23012.q: Which group of animals do trilobites belong to?
23012.e: Trilobites had jointed legs like crabs and insects. They belong to the arthropods.

23013.q: Were there trilobites before the dinosaurs?
a: No, at exactly the same time
23013.e: The first trilobites lived more than 500 million years ago. They had already died out when the dinosaurs came.
23013.m: Trilobites lived long before the dinosaurs.

23014.q: What did trilobites do when they grew?
23014.e: The hard shell could not grow with them. That is why trilobites shed it and formed a new one.

23015.q: What did the shell of an ammonite usually look like?
23015.e: The shell was usually rolled up into a flat spiral. It looks a little like a snail shell.

23016.q: Which animals living today are ammonites most closely related to?
23016.e: Ammonites were cephalopods. They had tentacles like a squid.
23016.m: Ammonites are related to squid and octopuses.

23018.q: How was the inside of an ammonite shell built?
23018.e: The chambers were separated by walls. They contained gas and helped the animal to float.
23018.m: An ammonite shell has many chambers.

23019.q: In which part of the shell did the ammonite animal live?
a: In the chamber at the very front
On the outside of the shell
In all the chambers at once
23019.e: The animal sat in the large living chamber at the front, by the opening. From there it stretched out its tentacles.
23019.m: The ammonite lived in the chamber at the front.

23020.q: Which horns does the shell of an ammonite remind us of?
23020.e: The name comes from the Egyptian god Ammon. He was shown with curved ram's horns.

23021.q: In which Swiss mountain range are ammonites often found?
23021.e: The limestone rocks of the Jura formed in a sea. The Jurassic period is even named after these mountains.
23021.m: Many ammonites are found in the Jura.

23022.q: Roughly how big did the biggest ammonites get?
23022.e: The biggest known ammonite was found in 1895 near Seppenrade in Germany. Its shell measures about 1.74 metres.

23023.q: What kind of animal was Meganeura?
23023.e: Meganeura was a huge insect that looked like a dragonfly. It is one of the biggest insects of all time.

23024.q: How big was the wingspan of Meganeura?
23024.e: Its wings together were about 66 to 70 centimetres across. That is about as wide as a pigeon's.
23024.m: Meganeura had a wingspan of about 70 centimetres.

23025.q: Did Meganeura live before or after the dinosaurs?
23025.e: Meganeura lived about 300 million years ago in the Carboniferous. The dinosaurs came much later.

23026.e: Like dragonflies today, Meganeura was a hunter. It caught other insects in flight.

23027.q: Why could insects probably grow so big back then?
23027.e: Researchers think there was more oxygen in the air. This helped large insects breathe better.
23027.m: More oxygen probably helped the giant insects.

23028.q: In which country was Meganeura discovered?
23028.e: The first fossils were found in the 1880s near Commentry in France.

23029.q: How many wings did Meganeura have?
23029.e: Like dragonflies today, Meganeura had two pairs of wings.

23030.q: How many legs did Meganeura have?
23030.e: Meganeura was an insect. All insects have six legs.

23031.q: What does the Latin word that “fossil” comes from mean?
23031.e: The Latin word “fossilis” means “dug up”. After all, fossils usually have to be taken out of the ground.
23031.m: The word fossil originally means dug up.

23032.e: Coprolites are fossilised droppings of animals. They show scientists what the animals ate.

23033.e: Palaeontologists want to know which animals and plants lived on Earth in the past. They find their traces in rocks.

23034.e: Fossils usually lie in layers of rock. These layers formed over a very long time.
23034.m: Fossils are usually found in rock.

23035.q: What do palaeontologists write down carefully when they make a find?
23035.e: The exact place of the find is very important. Only then do you know later which rock layer and which time a fossil comes from.
23035.m: Palaeontologists always note exactly where they found something.

23036.q: What does a fossilised dinosaur tooth show?
23036.e: Pointed teeth for tearing often belonged to meat eaters. Wide or leaf-shaped teeth usually belonged to plant eaters.
23036.m: Teeth reveal what an animal ate.

23037.e: Ammonites were sea animals with a shell coiled like a snail's. Their fossils are also often found in Switzerland.
23037.m: Ammonites were sea animals with a coiled shell.

23038.q: What do we call the preserved remains of prehistoric living things?
23038.e: Bones, shells, prints or traces of prehistoric living things preserved in rock are called fossils. Crystals and gemstones, on the other hand, were never alive.
23038.m: Fossils are remains of prehistoric living things.

23039.q: What do scientists use to look closely at tiny fossils?
23039.e: Some fossils are so small that you can hardly see them with the naked eye. A microscope makes them much bigger.
23039.m: With a microscope you can see even tiny fossils.

23040.q: What do you use to uncover a fossil very carefully?
23040.e: A fine brush sweeps away dust and earth. That way the fossil is not damaged.
23040.m: A brush is used to uncover fossils carefully.

23041.q: What is a shovel used for at a dig?
23041.e: First, a shovel is used to remove larger amounts of earth and rock. Close to the fossil, people then work with fine tools.
23041.m: A shovel is used first to move a lot of earth.

23042.q: Why is a fossil photographed before it is taken out?
a: So that its position is known
So that it does not fall apart
23042.e: Photos and drawings show how the bones lay in the ground. This helps later when putting them together and understanding them.
23042.m: The position of a find is recorded carefully before it is taken out.

23043.q: What are large bones wrapped in so that they do not break while being transported?
23043.e: Large bones are wrapped in strips of cloth and plaster. The hard covering protects them like a plaster cast.
23043.m: A plaster jacket protects large bones during transport.

23044.q: What is the place where scientists carefully search for fossils called?
23044.e: At an excavation site, the ground is carefully removed layer by layer. A dig often lasts several weeks.
23044.m: Scientists search for fossils at the excavation site.

23045.q: Why do people dig slowly at an excavation?
23045.e: Fossils are often fragile. If you dig too fast, you can destroy valuable finds.
23045.m: At an excavation, people work slowly and carefully.

23046.q: Where are the finds usually taken after an excavation?
23046.e: In the museum, the fossils are cleaned, studied and stored. Some are also put on display.
23046.m: Many fossils go to a museum after the dig.

23047.q: What does a preparator do with a fossil?
23047.e: Preparators remove the rock around the fossil in the laboratory. For this they need fine tools and a lot of patience.
23047.m: A preparator frees fossils from rock in the laboratory.

23048.q: What do people wear at a dig to protect their eyes?
23048.e: When tapping on rock, small splinters can fly off. Safety goggles protect the eyes from them.
23048.m: Safety goggles protect the eyes while working.

23049.q: Why is each find given a number?
a: So that it can be found again
23049.e: Each number belongs to notes about where it was found and the rock layer. That way the information about the find is never lost.
23049.m: Each find gets a number so that it can be found again.

23050.q: What happens to the bones when an animal becomes a fossil?
23050.e: Water in the ground carries minerals into the bones. Over a very long time, the bones become as hard as stone.
23050.m: When fossils form, bones slowly turn to stone.

23051.q: What must happen first to a dead animal so that it can become a fossil?
a: It lies in the sun for a long time
It is eaten by other animals
It dries out in the wind
23051.e: Mud or sand must cover the dead animal quickly. Then scavengers cannot destroy it.
23051.m: Only animals that are covered quickly can become fossils.

23052.q: Which parts of an animal become fossils most often?
23052.e: Hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells last the longest. Soft parts usually rot quickly.
23052.m: Hard parts such as bones become fossils best.

23053.q: How long does it take for a bone to become a fossil?
23053.e: Fossilisation usually takes thousands or millions of years. That is why fossils are so old.
23053.m: Becoming a fossil takes a very, very long time.

23054.q: Where do animals become fossils especially well?
a: At the bottom of lakes and seas
23054.e: Mud is always settling at the bottom of lakes and seas. It covers dead animals quickly.
23054.m: Many fossils form in the mud at the bottom of lakes and seas.

a: The shape of a living thing in stone
A picture that people scratched into stone
A bone that turned to stone
A stone with a hole in it
23055.e: Sometimes the living thing disappears completely, but its shape is preserved in the rock. This often happens with leaves and shells.
23055.m: An imprint shows the shape of a living thing in stone.

23056.q: What builds up over the years on top of a buried animal?
23056.e: Layer after layer of sand and mud settles on top. Under the pressure, the layers turn into rock.
23056.m: Many new layers form over buried animals.

23057.q: How does a fossil come back up to the surface from deep down?
23057.e: Wind, water and ice slowly wear rock away. Fossils also come to light during building work or in quarries.
23057.m: When rock is worn away, fossils come to light.

23058.q: Why are only a few animals ever found as fossils?
a: Most of them rot away completely
There used to be only a few animals
Animals used to live only in water
23058.e: Most dead animals are eaten or rot away. Only rarely are the conditions right for them to turn to stone.
23058.m: Only a few animals become fossils after they die.

23059.e: Amber is very old tree resin that has gone hard. It is often millions of years old.

23060.e: Most amber glows honey yellow to orange. But there are also lighter and darker pieces.
23060.m: Amber is usually yellow to orange.

23061.q: How did insects end up inside amber?
a: They got stuck in the resin
23061.e: Insects got stuck in the sticky resin. More resin flowed over them and sealed them in.
23061.m: Insects got stuck in the resin and were sealed in.

23062.q: What is special about insects in amber?
23062.e: In amber you can even see tiny legs, wings and hairs. The resin sealed them in airtight.
23062.m: Insects stay very well preserved in amber.

23063.q: On which sea's shores is a lot of amber found?
23063.e: People have collected amber on the beaches of the Baltic Sea for a very long time. It comes from prehistoric forests in that area.
23063.m: A lot of amber is found on the Baltic Sea.

23064.q: Apart from insects, what else can be found inside amber?
23064.e: As well as insects, amber can contain spiders, leaves, flowers or seeds. Big animals do not fit inside.
23064.m: Small bits of plants are also found in amber.

23065.q: What happens if you put amber in very salty water?
23065.e: Amber is very light, only a little heavier than water. In very salty water it floats on top; in fresh water it slowly sinks.
23065.m: Amber is so light that it floats in very salty water.

23066.q: What have people used amber for over a long time?
23066.e: People already wore amber as jewellery in the Stone Age. It is made into necklaces and pendants.
23066.m: Amber has been made into jewellery for a very long time.

23067.q: How does amber feel compared with a stone?
23067.e: Amber is much lighter than most stones. In your hand it feels rather warm.

23068.q: What is a fossilised dinosaur footprint?
23068.e: A dinosaur stepped in soft mud. The print was covered over and turned to stone over time.
23068.m: Dinosaur footprints are prints in stone.

23069.q: In what kind of ground did dinosaurs leave footprints?
23069.e: A foot only sinks into soft ground. Then the print had to dry and be covered over.
23069.m: Footprints were made in soft mud.

23070.q: What can you tell from many footprints one after another?
a: How fast the animal was moving
23070.e: If the footprints are far apart, the animal was running fast. Short gaps show slow walking.
23070.m: The gap between footprints shows how fast an animal was moving.

23071.q: What do many trackways side by side, all going the same way, show?
23071.e: When many trackways run side by side, several animals walked together. Some dinosaurs probably lived in herds.
23071.m: Many tracks going the same way show a group.

23072.q: In which Swiss canton is the Lommiswil quarry with dinosaur footprints?
23072.e: In the Lommiswil quarry you can see lots of dinosaur footprints on a sloping slab of rock. Lommiswil is in the canton of Solothurn.
23072.m: There are dinosaur footprints near Lommiswil in the canton of Solothurn.

23073.q: How many toes does the footprint of a meat-eating dinosaur usually show?
23073.e: Meat-eating dinosaurs walked on two legs. Their footprints usually show three toes, a bit like a bird's.
23073.m: Meat-eating dinosaurs usually left three-toed footprints.

23074.q: Which animals today have footprints similar to some dinosaurs?
23074.e: Birds are descended from dinosaurs. Their three-toed footprints look like small dinosaur footprints.
23074.m: Bird footprints look like some dinosaur footprints.

23075.q: What does a very large round footprint tell you?
23075.e: Large round prints often come from huge long-necked dinosaurs. They walked on four thick legs.
23075.m: Large round footprints come from heavy dinosaurs.

23076.q: Why are dinosaur footprints exciting for scientists?
a: They show how the animals moved
They show what colour the animals were
They show what the animals sounded like
They show what the animals were called
23076.e: Bones come from dead animals. Footprints, on the other hand, show how an animal lived and moved.

23077.q: Where can you look at dinosaur skeletons?
23077.e: Natural history museums display dinosaur skeletons. Often they are copies made from real bones.
23077.m: You can look at dinosaur skeletons in a museum.

23078.q: What are many of the skeletons in museums made of?
23078.e: Real bones are heavy and valuable. So museums often show light casts that look exactly the same.
23078.m: Museums often show casts instead of real bones.

23079.q: What holds a big skeleton upright in a museum?
23079.e: A metal frame carries the heavy bones. That way the skeleton can stand in a real pose.
23079.m: A metal frame holds big skeletons upright.

23080.q: What do you call the frame of bones in a body?
23080.e: The skeleton is made of many bones. It gives the body support and shape.
23080.m: The skeleton is the body's frame of bones.

23081.q: Which dinosaur is known for its short arms?
23081.e: Tyrannosaurus was a huge meat-eating dinosaur. Its arms were very short compared with its body.

23082.q: Which dinosaur had three horns on its head?
23082.e: The name Triceratops means “three-horned face”. It had two long horns above its eyes and one on its nose.
23082.m: Triceratops had three horns on its head.

23083.q: Which dinosaur had large plates on its back?
23083.e: Stegosaurus had two rows of large bony plates on its back. It had spikes on its tail.
23083.m: Stegosaurus had plates on its back.

23084.e: These dinosaurs had a very long neck and a long tail. They ate plants.
23084.m: Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus were long-necked dinosaurs.

23085.q: How do scientists build a skeleton when bones are missing?
23085.e: Missing bones are copied using related animals as a model. Good museums show which parts are real.
23085.m: Missing bones are replaced with copies.

23086.q: In which canton is the Dinosaur Museum in Frick?
23086.e: Frick is a village in the Fricktal valley in the canton of Aargau. Many dinosaur bones were found there.
23086.m: The Dinosaur Museum in Frick is in the canton of Aargau.

23087.q: What is the clay from the pit in Frick dug out for?
23087.e: A brickworks digs clay in Frick. While digging, workers came across the dinosaur bones.
23087.m: In Frick, clay is dug for roof tiles and bricks.

23088.e: Plateosaurus was a plant-eater. Its teeth and jaw show this.

23089.q: Where in Frick were the dinosaur bones found?
23089.e: The bones turned up in the Gruhalde clay pit. They lay in old layers of marl.
23089.m: The dinosaurs of Frick lay in a clay pit.

a: In the time of the lake dwellers
23090.e: Plateosaurus lived over 200 million years ago. There were no humans for a very long time after that.

23091.q: About how long could a fully grown Plateosaurus be?
23091.e: Fully grown Plateosaurus were about 5 to 10 metres long. That is as long as a lorry.
23091.m: Plateosaurus grew up to about 10 metres long.

23092.q: According to what we know today, how did Plateosaurus walk?
23092.e: People used to think it walked on four legs. Today scientists think it always walked on its back legs.

23093.q: Which dinosaur was found especially often in Frick?
23093.e: In Frick, bones of many Plateosaurus were found. That is why it is the star of the Dinosaur Museum.
23093.m: Many Plateosaurus were found in Frick.

23094.q: What is the showpiece of the Dinosaur Museum in Frick?
23094.e: In 1985 a complete, joined-up Plateosaurus skeleton was found in Frick. It is the centrepiece of the museum.
23094.m: A whole Plateosaurus skeleton is the showpiece in Frick.

23095.q: In which canton is Monte San Giorgio?
23095.e: Monte San Giorgio is in the far south of Switzerland. It is a wooded mountain in the canton of Ticino.
23095.m: Monte San Giorgio is in Ticino.

23096.q: What is Monte San Giorgio famous for?
23096.e: Very many well-preserved fossils were found on Monte San Giorgio. They come from the Triassic.
23096.m: Monte San Giorgio is famous for its fossils.

23097.q: With which neighbouring country does Switzerland share the Monte San Giorgio World Heritage Site?
23097.e: The mountain lies on the border. In 2010 the Italian part was also added to the World Heritage Site.
23097.m: The Monte San Giorgio World Heritage Site belongs to Switzerland and Italy.

23098.q: On which lake is Monte San Giorgio?
23098.e: Monte San Giorgio rises on the southern shore of Lake Lugano. From the top you can see far across the lake.
23098.m: Monte San Giorgio is on Lake Lugano.

23099.q: Which animals are mainly found on Monte San Giorgio?
23099.e: About 240 million years ago there was a sea bay here. That is why many fish and sea reptiles are found.
23099.m: Fish and sea reptiles are found on Monte San Giorgio.

23100.q: What was at Monte San Giorgio at the time of the fossils?
23100.e: In the Triassic there was a warm sea basin there. After they died, the animals sank to the bottom and were covered with mud.
23100.m: Where Monte San Giorgio is today, there used to be a sea.

23101.q: In which village on Monte San Giorgio is there a fossil museum?
23101.e: The fossil museum is in Meride. The architect Mario Botta redesigned it, and it reopened in 2012.
23101.m: The Monte San Giorgio fossil museum is in Meride.

23102.q: What was Mixosaurus from Monte San Giorgio?
23102.e: Mixosaurus was an ichthyosaur about one metre long that swam in the sea. Several hundred of them were found on Monte San Giorgio.
23102.m: Mixosaurus was an ichthyosaur from the sea.

23103.q: In which city are most of the finds from Monte San Giorgio kept today?
23103.e: Most fossils from Monte San Giorgio are kept at the University of Zurich. Many of them are on display in its museum.
23103.m: Many finds from Monte San Giorgio are in Zurich.

23104.q: Which country did the fossil collector Mary Anning come from?
23104.e: Mary Anning lived in Lyme Regis on the south coast of England. There she searched the cliffs for fossils.
23104.m: Mary Anning collected fossils in England.

23105.q: Where did Mary Anning look for fossils?
23105.e: The cliffs near Lyme Regis crumble in storms. Again and again, fossils come to light.
23105.m: Mary Anning searched cliffs by the sea.

23106.q: In which century did Mary Anning live?
23106.e: Mary Anning was born in 1799 and died in 1847. So she lived almost entirely in the 19th century.
23106.m: Mary Anning lived in the 19th century.

23107.q: Which skeleton did Mary Anning find with her brother when she was still a child?
23107.e: Around 1811, Mary and her brother Joseph found the skeleton of an Ichthyosaurus. That is a fish-like sea reptile.
23107.m: Mary Anning found an ichthyosaur as a child.

23108.q: What did Mary Anning do with many of her finds?
23108.e: Her family was poor. Mary sold fossils to collectors and scientists to earn money.

23109.q: Which long-necked sea animal did Mary Anning find in 1823?
23109.e: Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur. These sea reptiles had a long neck and four flippers.
23109.m: Mary Anning found a long-necked plesiosaur.

23110.q: What special fossil did Mary Anning find in 1828?
23110.e: She discovered the skeleton of a flying reptile, later named Dimorphodon. It was the first such find in Great Britain.
23110.m: Mary Anning also found a flying reptile.

23111.q: Why was Mary Anning given little credit in her time?
23111.e: Back then, women were not allowed to join scientific societies. Others often got the fame for her finds.
23111.m: As a woman, Mary Anning was given too little credit in her time.

23112.q: What did Mary Anning become, even though she was never allowed to study?
23112.e: Mary Anning taught herself everything and knew a great deal about fossils. Today she is seen as an important pioneer of palaeontology.
23112.m: Without any studies, Mary Anning became a well-known scientist.

23113.e: Coal comes from plants in huge prehistoric swamp forests. Over millions of years they turned into coal.
23113.m: Coal was formed from prehistoric plants.

23114.q: In what kind of landscape did the plants that became coal grow?
23114.e: In wet swamps, fallen trees dropped into the water. There they did not rot away completely.
23114.m: Coal comes from prehistoric swamp forests.

23115.e: Coal is black and often a little shiny. It is mainly made of carbon.

23116.q: Which plants grew in the coal forests?
23116.e: Tree-sized ferns, horsetails and club mosses grew in the coal forests. There were no flowers yet.
23116.m: Giant ferns grew in the coal forests.

23117.q: What fossils are sometimes found in coal?
23117.e: In coal and the rock next to it you often see prints of fern leaves. They show the plants of prehistoric times.
23117.m: Leaf prints are often found in coal.

23118.q: What was coal often burnt for in the past?
23118.e: Coal burns for a long time and gives off a lot of heat. It was used to heat houses and run steam engines.
23118.m: In the past, people often heated with coal.

23119.q: How is coal taken out of the ground?
23119.e: Coal is dug in mines, underground or in big open pits. The workers are called miners.
23119.m: Coal is taken out of the ground in a mine.

23120.q: What is the geological period of the great coal forests called?
23120.e: The Carboniferous is named after the Latin word for coal. At this time, huge swamp forests grew.
23120.m: The Carboniferous is the time of the coal forests.

23121.q: What forms from plants in bogs today?
23121.e: In bogs, plants break down only slowly. Peat forms, an early stage of coal.
23121.m: Peat forms from plants in bogs.

23122.q: In which order did the periods of the dinosaurs follow each other?
23122.e: First came the Triassic, then the Jurassic and finally the Cretaceous. Together they are called the Mesozoic Era.
23122.m: The age of the dinosaurs began with the Triassic and ended with the Cretaceous.

23123.q: Which of these dinosaurs lived in the Jurassic?
23123.e: Stegosaurus lived in the late Jurassic, around 150 million years ago. The other three dinosaurs lived at other times.

23124.q: About when did the Triassic begin?
23124.e: The Triassic began about 252 million years ago. That is unimaginably long ago.
23124.m: The Triassic began around 250 million years ago.

23125.q: Where does the Cretaceous period get its name from?
23125.e: At this time, thick layers of white chalk formed. They are made of the tiny shells of sea creatures.
23125.m: The Cretaceous is named after white chalk rock.

23126.q: What probably ended the age of the dinosaurs?
23126.e: About 66 million years ago a large object from space hit the Earth. The climate changed a lot.
23126.m: A meteorite probably ended the age of the dinosaurs.

23127.q: Did humans live at the same time as the dinosaurs?
23127.e: The big dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. Humans have only existed for a few hundred thousand years.
23127.m: Humans and dinosaurs never lived at the same time.

23128.q: What are the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous called together?
23128.e: The Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous make up the Mesozoic Era. Experts also call it the Earth's middle age.
23128.m: Together, the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous form the Mesozoic Era.

23129.q: In which period did Tyrannosaurus live?
23129.e: Tyrannosaurus lived at the very end of the Cretaceous. It was one of the last big dinosaurs.

23130.q: Who has lived longer: the dinosaurs or, so far, humans?
23130.e: Dinosaurs existed for over 150 million years. Humans have only existed for a tiny fraction of that time.
23130.m: Dinosaurs lived on Earth much longer than humans have so far.

23131.q: What do you call animal skin that has been made soft and long-lasting?
23131.e: Animal skin is turned into leather by working on it. Leather is soft, strong and lasts a long time.
23131.m: Leather is made from animal skin.

23132.q: What did people first scrape off the inside of a fresh animal skin?
23132.e: Bits of meat and fat still stuck to a fresh skin. They had to come off, or the skin would rot.
23132.m: A fresh skin has to be scraped clean first.

23133.q: What did people in the Old Stone Age use to scrape a skin clean?
23133.e: A scraper is a stone tool with a round, sharp edge. It was used to scrape bits off the skin.
23133.m: The skin was cleaned with a stone scraper.

23134.q: What is the work called that makes animal skin long-lasting?
23134.e: In tanning, the skin is treated so that it does not rot and stays soft. That is how leather is made.

23135.q: What had not yet been invented in the Old Stone Age?
23135.e: The loom only came much later, in the New Stone Age. In the Old Stone Age people mainly wore clothes made of fur and leather.
23135.m: There was no loom yet in the Old Stone Age.

23136.q: What did Ice Age people probably wear on their feet when it was cold?
a: Shoes made of fur and leather
23136.e: Soft shoes made of leather and fur helped against cold and snow. Rubber and wooden shoes were unknown then.
23136.m: In winter, fur shoes protected the feet.

23137.q: What did people in the Old Stone Age use to fasten a fur coat?
23137.e: There was no woven cloth or metal yet. Clothes were tied shut with leather straps.
23137.m: Leather straps held fur clothes together.

23138.q: Why are clothes from the Old Stone Age hardly ever found today?
a: Fur and leather have rotted away
Nobody has ever looked for them
23138.e: Fur and leather break down in the ground over time. Stone tools, on the other hand, last for many thousands of years.
23138.m: Fur clothes break down in the ground.

23139.q: Which animals provided warm furs in the Ice Age?
23139.e: Animals from cold places have thick fur. So reindeer and foxes were good for warm clothes.
23139.m: Animals with thick fur provided warm clothes.

23140.q: What is the hole in a sewing needle called?
23140.e: You thread the thread through the eye. Even needles from the Old Stone Age had a hole like this.
23140.m: The thread goes through the eye of the needle.

23141.q: What did people in the Old Stone Age use as thread for sewing?
23141.e: Animal sinew can be dried and split into thin threads. These threads are very hard to tear.
23141.m: Strong threads were made from animal sinew.

23142.q: What did people need a bone needle for?
23142.e: With a needle and thread, pieces of fur could be joined. That is how clothes, shoes and bags were made.
23142.m: Pieces of fur were sewn together with a bone needle.

23143.q: What did people use to bore the hole in a bone needle?
23143.e: A pointed piece of flint is hard enough to twist a hole into bone. Metal was not yet known.
23143.m: Small holes were bored with pointed stones.

23144.q: How did people make a bone needle smooth and pointed?
a: They ground it on a rough stone
They put it in the fire
They left it out in the rain
23144.e: You rub the bone back and forth on a rough stone. That makes it smooth, thin and pointed.
23144.m: The needle was ground on a rough stone.

23145.q: Which clothes could be made better thanks to the sewing needle?
a: Clothes that fit close to the body
Loose capes made of one skin
23145.e: With needle and thread, pieces could be sewn together exactly. Close-fitting clothes keep you much warmer than loose furs.

23146.q: About how long was a bone needle?
a: About as long as a finger
About as long as an arm
About as long as a leg
About as long as a bike
23146.e: Most needles that have been found are only a few centimetres long. So they are about finger-length and very fine.
23146.m: Bone needles were small and fine.

23147.q: What is a pointed tool for punching holes in leather called?
23147.e: You punch holes in thick leather with an awl. Then it is easier to pull the thread through.
23147.m: An awl punches holes in leather.

23148.q: Apart from clothes, what else did people sew?
23148.e: A tent needed large covers made of many skins. These were sewn together. Nets were knotted and baskets were woven.
23148.m: Tent covers were also sewn from skins.

a: A long pole with a point
23149.e: A spear is a long pole with a sharp point. You can stab with it or throw it.
23149.m: A spear is a long pole with a point.

23150.q: What were the oldest spears ever found made of?
23150.e: In Schöningen in Germany, wooden spears about 200,000 to 300,000 years old were found. They were preserved in wet ground.
23150.m: The oldest spears were made of wood.

23151.q: What could you do with a spear?
a: Throw it or stab with it
23151.e: A spear was a hunting weapon. You threw it at an animal or stabbed with it from close up.
23151.m: You could throw and stab with a spear.

a: It makes the spear fly further
It sets the spear on fire
23152.e: The spear-thrower helps with throwing. The spear flies faster and further than with your hand alone.
23152.m: With a spear-thrower, the spear flies further.

23153.q: What does a spear-thrower have at one end?
23153.e: The back end of the spear rests against the hook. When you throw, the hook pushes the spear forward.
23153.m: The spear rests against the hook of the spear-thrower.

23154.q: What did people often carve spear-throwers from?
23154.e: Many spear-throwers that have been found are carved from antler. There were probably wooden ones too.
23154.m: Spear-throwers were often carved from antler.

23155.q: What did people sometimes carve on a spear-thrower as decoration?
23155.e: Some spear-throwers have animals such as horses or ibexes carved on them. There was no writing yet.
23155.m: Some spear-throwers were decorated with animals.

23156.q: How does a spear-thrower work when throwing?
23156.e: The spear-thrower works like an extension of your arm. With a longer arm you can give much more swing.

23157.q: Why was hunting with a spear-thrower safer?
a: You did not have to get so close to the animal
23157.e: Because the spear flies far, the hunter could keep his distance. That way he was better protected from horns and hooves.
23157.m: Hunting from a distance was safer.

23158.q: What is the tight string on a bow called?
23158.e: The string on a bow is called the bowstring. It is pulled back and then snaps forward with the arrow.
23158.m: The string on a bow is called the bowstring.

23159.q: What did people in the Stone Age make the bow itself from?
23159.e: A bow must be bendy and strong. Wood is best for this.
23159.m: A bow is made from bendy wood.

23160.q: What was fixed to the back end of an arrow so it flew straight?
23160.e: Feathers at the end of the arrow keep it steady in flight. That way it hits better.
23160.m: Feathers make the arrow fly straight.

23161.q: What did people use to glue an arrowhead onto an arrow?
23161.e: Birch tar is made by heating birch bark. It is a strong glue from the Stone Age.
23161.m: Birch tar was the glue of the Stone Age.

23162.q: What is one advantage of a bow and arrow over a spear?
a: You can shoot many arrows quickly
23162.e: A hunter can carry many arrows. He can shoot them quickly one after another.
23162.m: With a bow you can shoot many arrows one after another.

23163.q: What is the container for carrying arrows called?
23163.e: The arrows go in the quiver. It is usually carried on the back or at the side.
23163.m: Arrows are carried in a quiver.

23164.q: Very old wooden arrows were found in Stellmoor in northern Germany. Which animals did people mainly hunt there?
23164.e: Stellmoor was a hunting place at the end of the Ice Age. Very many reindeer bones were found there.
23164.m: In Stellmoor, people hunted reindeer with bow and arrow.

23165.q: What do you call someone who shoots with a bow and arrow?
23165.e: Someone who shoots with a bow is an archer. Today archery is also a sport.
23165.m: An archer shoots with a bow and arrow.

23166.q: Which part of Stone Age arrows is found most often today?
23166.e: Wood, feathers and leather usually break down in the ground. Stone points, on the other hand, survive.
23166.m: Stone arrowheads are still found today.

23167.q: Which nuts could gatherers find in Europe?
23167.e: Hazel bushes grow here in Europe. Coconuts, peanuts and Brazil nuts come from warm countries far away.

23168.q: What is a pointed stick for digging up roots called?
23168.e: A digging stick was used to loosen the soil. That way people could get at roots and tubers.
23168.m: You dig up roots with a digging stick.

23169.q: What did gatherers dig out of the ground?
23169.e: Many plants store food in their roots and tubers. These could be eaten, often cooked or roasted.
23169.m: Roots were also food for gatherers.

23170.q: Why did people have to be careful when picking berries?
a: Berries only grow very high up
23170.e: Not all berries can be eaten; some make you ill. The adults showed the children which ones were good.

23171.q: What did gatherers in the Old Stone Age carry their berries in?
23171.e: There was no plastic, glass or tin yet. But bags could be sewn from leather.
23171.m: Gatherers carried their food in leather bags.

23172.q: When did gatherers find the most berries?
23172.e: Berries ripen in summer and autumn. In winter people had to live on other food.
23172.m: Berries ripen in summer and autumn.

23173.q: Apart from plants, what else did people gather?
23173.e: People found birds' eggs in nests. Bread, cheese and milk only came once people grew grain and kept animals.

23174.q: What did brave gatherers take from wild bees?
23174.e: Wild bees build their honeycombs in hollow trees. Sweet honey was a rare and popular food.
23174.m: Honey was taken from wild bees.

23175.q: What does a harpoon have at its tip so the fish does not slip off?
23175.e: Barbs are small spikes pointing backwards. They hold the fish tight.
23175.m: Barbs hold the fish on the harpoon.

23176.q: Which fish did people in the Old Stone Age catch in rivers?
23176.e: Salmon swim up rivers. Sharks, tuna and herring live in the sea.

23177.q: Where did people usually fish with a harpoon?
a: In shallow water near the bank
In the middle of the deep sea
23177.e: In shallow, clear water you can see the fish well. There they could be hit with a harpoon.
23177.m: Harpoon fishing was done in shallow water.

23178.q: When could fishers catch especially many salmon?
a: When they were swimming up the river
In the middle of cold winter
When it had not rained for a long time
23178.e: Salmon swim upstream in large groups to lay eggs. Then there were lots of fish all at once.
23178.m: Migrating salmon were easy to catch.

23179.q: What is the long pole that the harpoon point is attached to called?
23179.e: The shaft is the long wooden pole. The point with the barbs is fixed at the front.
23179.m: The long pole of a harpoon is called the shaft.

23180.q: Apart from harpoons, what else did people fish with?
23180.e: Small hooks were carved from bone or shells. There was no metal yet.
23180.m: Bone fish hooks were also used for fishing.

23181.q: What did people in the Old Stone Age carve their harpoon points from?
23181.e: Harpoon points were carved from reindeer antler or bone. Metal was not yet known.
23181.m: Harpoon points were made of antler or bone.

23182.q: What did a fisher with a harpoon need to be good at?
23182.e: Fish get frightened easily. The fisher had to stand still and strike accurately at the right moment.
23182.m: Fishing with a harpoon takes patience.

23183.q: What did people in Eastern Europe build huts from in the Ice Age?
23183.e: The remains of round huts were found in Eastern Europe. Their walls were made of many large mammoth bones.
23183.m: Some huts were built from mammoth bones.

23184.q: Why did people there build with bones instead of wood?
23184.e: Only a few trees grew on the cold Ice Age steppe. But there were plenty of mammoth bones.
23184.m: Where there were no trees, people built with bones.

23185.q: What did people cover a mammoth-bone hut with?
23185.e: Skins were laid over the frame of bones. That made the huts tight against wind and cold.

23186.q: In which present-day country were many mammoth-bone huts found?
23186.e: Well-known sites such as Mezhyrich are in Ukraine. Many mammoths lived there in the Ice Age.
23186.m: Many mammoth-bone huts were found in Ukraine.

23187.q: What else did people burn instead of wood on the treeless steppe?
23187.e: Bones contain fat and can burn. Because there was no wood, they were used as fuel.
23187.m: Where there was no wood, people burnt bones.

23188.q: Where did people get many of the mammoth bones for their huts?
a: They also collected bones of dead mammoths
They found them in the sea
23188.e: Not all mammoths were hunted. Bones of animals that were already dead were collected too.
23188.m: Bones of dead mammoths were collected too.

23189.q: About how old are the mammoth-bone huts from Ukraine?
23189.e: The huts date from the last Ice Age, about 15,000 years ago. 15 million years ago there were no humans yet.
23189.m: The mammoth-bone huts are about 15,000 years old.

23190.q: What was there in a mammoth-bone hut to keep out the cold?
23190.e: A fire burnt in the hut. It gave warmth and light.

23191.e: An abri is a place where the top of a rock face sticks far out. Underneath, you are sheltered.
23191.m: An abri is a rock shelter.

23192.q: Which language does the word “abri” come from?
23192.e: “Abri” is French and means shelter or refuge.
23192.m: Abri is the French word for shelter.

23193.q: What did a rock shelter protect people from?
23193.e: The rock overhead keeps off rain and snow. The rock face behind you slows down the wind.
23193.m: Under a rock shelter you are protected from the weather.

23194.q: What was better under a rock shelter than deep inside a cave?
a: It was lighter and the smoke could escape
It was better protected from wind
23194.e: A rock shelter is open at the front. Daylight gets in and the smoke from the fire can escape.
23194.m: It was light under a rock shelter.

23195.q: What is a well-known Stone Age living place under a rock shelter near Schaffhausen called?
23195.e: At the end of the Ice Age, hunters lived under a rock shelter at Schweizersbild. Wildkirchli, Cotencher and Drachenloch are caves in other cantons.
23195.m: Schweizersbild near Schaffhausen is a Stone Age rock shelter.

23196.q: Which position was especially pleasant for a rock shelter in winter?
a: In the middle of a river
23196.e: On the sunny side, the sun warms the rock. So it is less cold there.
23196.m: A rock shelter on the sunny side is warmer.

23197.q: What do archaeologists often find in the ground under rock shelters?
23197.e: People left rubbish and tools lying around. They survived in the ground for many thousands of years.
23197.m: Traces of the Stone Age lie in the ground under rock shelters.

23198.q: Did people live under the same rock shelter all year round?
a: No, often only for a while
No, never longer than an hour
23198.e: People moved on when food ran short. A rock shelter was often just a resting place for a while.
23198.m: People usually lived under rock shelters only for a while.

23199.e: With reindeer, the females have antlers too. With other deer, usually only the males have them.
23199.m: With reindeer, the females have antlers too.

23200.q: How much of a reindeer did hunters use?
23200.e: The meat was for eating, the fur for clothes, antlers and bones for tools and sinews for thread.
23200.m: Almost every part of a reindeer was used.

23201.q: In which country do many reindeer live today?
23201.e: Today reindeer live in the cold north, for example in Finland, Norway and Sweden.

23202.q: What are wild reindeer called in North America?
23202.e: Reindeer and caribou are the same species. In North America they are called caribou.
23202.m: Caribou are reindeer from North America.

23203.q: Where did hunters like to lie in wait for reindeer herds?
a: Where the herd crossed a river
In the middle of a forest
23203.e: When swimming across a river, the animals move only slowly. Then they were easier to hunt.
23203.m: Reindeer were hunted at river crossings.

23204.q: What do reindeer often eat in winter?
23204.e: Reindeer scrape away the snow with their hooves. Underneath they find lichens, which are also called reindeer moss.

23205.q: Which animal is the reindeer related to?
23205.e: The reindeer belongs to the deer family. That is why it has antlers too.
23205.m: The reindeer is a kind of deer.

23206.q: Why do reindeer hardly sink into the snow?
23206.e: Reindeer have wide, spread-out hooves. These carry them over the snow like snowshoes.
23206.m: Wide hooves carry the reindeer over the snow.

23207.q: How did people make a necklace out of shells?
a: They bored holes and threaded them
They melted them in the fire
23207.e: A small hole was bored in each shell. Then a string was pulled through.
23207.m: For a necklace, you bore holes in the shells.

23208.q: Which animal teeth did people in the Old Stone Age like to wear as jewellery?
23208.e: Many fox teeth with holes bored in them have been found. They were worn as pendants.
23208.m: Fox teeth with holes were popular jewellery.

23209.q: Sea shells have been found far away from the sea. What does this show?
a: People traded them or brought them along
23209.e: The shells did not get inland by themselves. People carried them or traded them with other groups.
23209.m: Jewellery shells were carried far or traded.

23210.q: What was the string for a necklace often made of in the Stone Age?
23210.e: Thin straps could be cut from leather. Shells and teeth were threaded onto them.
23210.m: Necklaces were threaded on leather straps.

23211.q: What did some Stone Age people sew onto their clothes as decoration?
23211.e: Thousands of small beads made of shell or ivory have been found in old graves. They were sewn onto the clothes.

23212.q: Which material did Ice Age people carve beautiful beads from?
23212.e: Ivory from mammoth tusks is easy to carve. Metals such as gold, silver and bronze were not yet known.
23212.m: Beads were also carved from ivory.

23213.q: Why did people in the Old Stone Age probably wear jewellery?
a: To look nice and show who they were
23213.e: Jewellery is no use for hunting. Scientists think it looked nice and showed which group someone belonged to.
23213.m: Even back then, jewellery showed who you were.

23214.q: Which empty animal homes were also used as beads?
23214.e: Small snail shells can be bored through and threaded. They have often been found in Stone Age necklaces.
23214.m: Snail shells were worn as beads.

23215.e: In a clan, people live together who are related to each other. This includes parents, children, grandparents and other relatives.
23215.m: A clan is a group of relatives.

23216.q: Why did people in the Old Stone Age live in groups?
a: It was easier to survive together
You were not allowed to make fire alone
23216.e: In a group you could hunt big animals and help each other. Alone, life was much more dangerous.
23216.m: It was easier to survive together.

23217.q: About how big was a clan?
23217.e: A clan was usually a small group. A big group would not have found enough food in one place.
23217.m: A clan was a small group.

23218.q: How did children learn in the Old Stone Age?
a: With a teacher in the village
23218.e: There were no schools or writing yet. Children watched the adults and helped out.
23218.m: Children learnt by watching and joining in.

23219.q: Who passed on their knowledge to the children?
a: The adults and the old people
23219.e: The older people knew where to find water and berries and how to hunt. They told the young ones about it.
23219.m: The old people passed on their knowledge.

23220.q: What did the clan do with the catch after a hunt?
23220.e: The meat of a big animal was enough for many people. It was shared with everyone in the group.
23220.m: In the clan, food was shared.

23221.q: Where did the clan often sit together in the evening?
a: In the water at the river
In a pit in the forest
23221.e: The fire gave light and warmth. There people ate and told each other stories.
23221.m: In the evening the clan sat by the fire.

23222.q: What did the clan probably do when someone was injured?
23222.e: Skeletons with healed serious injuries have been found. These people were cared for by others.
23222.m: Injured people were looked after by the group.

23223.q: What did reindeer herds do in spring and autumn?
a: They stayed in the same place
23223.e: Reindeer move back and forth between summer and winter areas. The hunters followed them.
23223.m: Reindeer herds travel long distances every year.

23224.q: How did people in the Old Stone Age transport their belongings?
23224.e: There were no carts and no tame horses yet. Everything had to be carried on your back or in your arms.

23225.q: Why did people who moved around a lot have only a few belongings?
23225.e: If you often move on, you cannot take much with you. So people only owned what they really needed.
23225.m: If you move around a lot, you have little luggage.

23226.q: What did people take from their tent when they moved on?
23226.e: The skins were valuable and light enough to carry. At the new place they were used to build a tent again.
23226.m: When moving on, people took the tent skins with them.

23227.q: How did people know where the herds would go?
23227.e: The herds took similar routes every year. The old people knew these routes and told others about them.
23227.m: Experience showed hunters the routes of the herds.

23228.q: Did people sometimes come back to old camps?
a: Yes, often at the same time of year
Yes, but only once in a lifetime
23228.e: Good places were used again and again. People came back when animals or plants could be found there at the right time.
23228.m: Good camps were visited again and again.

23229.q: How did people in the Old Stone Age travel long distances?
23229.e: Horses and reindeer were only tamed much later, and there were no carts yet. People in the Old Stone Age walked everywhere.
23229.m: In the Old Stone Age, people went everywhere on foot.

a: A place where you live for a while
23230.e: At the camp, the group put up its tents. When it moved on, it looked for a new camp.
23230.m: At a camp, you live for a while.

23231.q: What is the most famous room in the Lascaux cave called?
23231.e: In the Hall of the Bulls, large aurochs, horses and deer are painted on the walls and ceiling.
23231.m: The Hall of the Bulls is the best-known room at Lascaux.

23232.q: Next to which animal is a human painted in the shaft at Lascaux?
23232.e: In the deep shaft of the cave you see a bison that has been hit by a spear. Next to it lies a man with a bird's head.
23232.m: In the shaft at Lascaux, a man is painted next to a bison.

23233.q: Which animal with antlers is painted at Lascaux?
23233.e: At Lascaux you can see, among other things, a row of deer heads with large antlers.

23234.q: What is mainly painted on the walls of the Lascaux cave?
23234.e: At Lascaux you mainly see horses, aurochs and deer.
23234.m: At Lascaux, people mainly painted animals.

23235.q: Which large type of cattle is often painted at Lascaux?
23235.e: The aurochs was a large wild ox. One painted bull at Lascaux is over 5 metres long.
23235.m: The aurochs is a prehistoric wild ox.

23236.q: Why are visitors no longer allowed into the real Lascaux cave?
23236.e: The breath of many visitors brought damp and mould into the cave. That is why it was closed in 1963.
23236.m: The real Lascaux cave stays closed to protect the paintings.

23237.q: What can visitors see at Lascaux today?
23237.e: The cave and its paintings have been copied exactly. The newest copy is called Lascaux IV and opened in 2016.
23237.m: At Lascaux today, you visit a copy of the cave.

23238.q: About how old are the paintings in the Lascaux cave?
23238.e: The paintings were made in the Old Stone Age, about 17,000 years ago.
23238.m: The paintings at Lascaux are many thousands of years old.

23239.q: In which country is the Chauvet Cave?
23239.e: The Chauvet Cave is in the south of France, near the River Ardèche.
23239.m: The Chauvet Cave is a cave in France.

23240.q: When was the Chauvet Cave discovered?
23240.e: Three cavers found the cave in December 1994.
23240.m: The Chauvet Cave was discovered in 1994.

23241.q: Where does the Chauvet Cave get its name from?
23241.e: One of the three discoverers was called Jean-Marie Chauvet. The cave is named after him.
23241.m: The Chauvet Cave bears the name of its discoverer.

23242.q: Which big cats are painted in the Chauvet Cave?
23242.e: In the Chauvet Cave you can see whole groups of cave lions.
23242.m: Lions are painted in the Chauvet Cave.

23243.q: Which animal with a horn on its nose is painted in the Chauvet Cave?
23243.e: Several woolly rhinoceroses are painted in the cave. They also lived in Europe at that time.
23243.m: Rhinoceroses also used to live in Europe.

23244.q: Which animal's bones and skulls lie in large numbers on the floor of the Chauvet Cave?
23244.e: Cave bears spent their winter rest in the Chauvet Cave. Many of their skulls and even paw prints have been found.
23244.m: Cave bears slept in the Chauvet Cave.

23245.q: About how old are the oldest paintings in the Chauvet Cave?
23245.e: Tests on the charcoal show that the oldest paintings are over 30,000 years old.
23245.m: The paintings of the Chauvet Cave are among the oldest in the world.

23246.q: Why is the Chauvet Cave so important for research?
a: It contains some of the oldest cave paintings in the world
The first iron tool was found there
It is the deepest cave in the world
